Gift
GIFT
n. (rendering Hebrew mattānâh, minchâh, and Greek dōrea, charisma)
From Old Norse gift, related to Old English giefu and to the verb give; the root sense is simply a giving. The Greek is more precise than the English and the New Testament exploits it: dōron is a present, dōrea a free gift with the emphasis on its gratuity, and charisma a gift of grace — formed directly on charis, grace, so that a charisma is grace taking a particular shape in a particular person.

Biblical Definition

The word gift carries the doctrine of grace in miniature, because a gift by definition is not wages. Paul builds the whole contrast on it: “the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom 6:23) — one side of the sentence is earned and paid, the other is given, and the two halves cannot be blended. He states it again with every avenue of self-congratulation closed: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and adds, not of works, lest any man should boast. The Lord Jesus uses the word of Himself and of the Spirit at the well — “If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink” (Joh 4:10) — where the woman's ignorance, not her unworthiness, is what stands between her and living water. James then extends the principle to the whole of providence: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17). Nothing good comes from any other quarter, and the Giver does not change — which is the ground of assurance, since a gift is only as secure as the constancy of the one who gave it. Scripture also speaks of gifts distributed for service, dividing to every man severally as the Spirit will, and of the unspeakable gift for which no name is adequate.

Webster 1828 Definition

A thing freely bestowed; in Scripture the governing word for salvation as opposed to wages, the term for Christ and the Spirit given to sinners, the description of every good thing in providence as descending from an unchanging Father, and the name of graces distributed for service.

expand to see more

GIFT, n. 1. A present; any thing given or bestowed; any thing the property of which is voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation.

2. The act of giving or conferring. The gift of God is eternal life. Rom. 6.

3. A bribe; something given to corrupt the judgment. A gift doth blind the eyes of the wise. Deut. 16. In this sense the law strictly forbids the receiving of gifts by judges.

4. A faculty or power bestowed; as the gifts of the Spirit, distributed to every man severally as he will. 1 Cor. 12.

5. In law, a gift is distinguished from a sale or exchange in that no price or consideration passes; whence the theological use, that salvation given for a price would not be a gift at all.

Key Scripture

Romans 6:23 — "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Ephesians 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

John 4:10 — "Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water."

James 1:17 — "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

Modern Corruption

The freeness of the gift is undone in two directions: by systems that attach a price or a condition of merit to it, and by a cheap-grace preaching that keeps the word gift while dropping the repentance and faith by which it is actually received.

expand to see more

Any scheme in which salvation is partly earned has ceased to describe a gift, whatever it calls itself. Rome's treasury of merit, its indulgences, and its insistence that justification is by an infused righteousness cooperated with, all attach a price; and the Reformation's recovery was precisely at this point, that we are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. But the same error grows readily on Protestant soil in subtler forms — where assurance is made to rest on the quality of one's repentance, the intensity of one's experience, or the consistency of one's service, the gift has quietly become a wage again. Isaiah's invitation is the standing rebuke: come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

The opposite abuse keeps the vocabulary of gift and empties it of everything else. If salvation is free, it is argued, then nothing follows from it, and repentance, obedience, and perseverance become optional extras. Scripture never separates what it distinguishes. The gift is received by faith, and the faith that receives it is itself God's gift and is never alone in the person justified; Eph 2:8-9 is immediately followed by Eph 2:10, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Works are excluded from the ground of salvation and required as its fruit. A gift that leaves the recipient wholly unchanged was not this gift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mattānâh is a present or offering; minchâh is a tribute or meat offering. Greek distinguishes dōron (a present), dōrea (a free gift), and charisma (a gift of grace), all three used deliberately in the epistles.

expand to see more

Hebrew mattānâh (H4979) — a gift, a present; used of gifts among men and of the Levites given as a gift for the service of the tabernacle (Num 18:6).

Hebrew minchâh (H4503) — a gift, tribute, or meat offering; the word for Cain's and Abel's offerings in Gen 4.

Greek dōrea (G1431) — a free gift, with stress on its gratuity; used of the gift of the Holy Ghost (Act 2:38) and of the unspeakable gift (2Co 9:15).

Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; formed on charis, grace. Used of eternal life (Rom 6:23) and of gifts for service (1Co 12:4).

Greek opsonion (G3800) — a soldier's rations or wages; the word set against charisma in Rom 6:23 — sin pays, God gives.

Usage

"Of salvation as opposed to wages: the gift of God is eternal life (Rom 6:23); it is the gift of God, not of works (Eph 2:8-9)."

"Of Christ and the Spirit given: the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee (Joh 4:10); ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost (Act 2:38)."

"Of providence and of service: every good gift is from above (Jas 1:17); having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us (Rom 12:6)."
